title: Base, posture, balance, and leverage
note: You stay standing while your center of gravity stays over your base of support. Posture keeps head, spine, and hips aligned so force travels through the skeleton. Kuzushi, breaking the partner's balance, comes before a throw, and a lever multiplies force when it is applied far from its pivot.

read.title: How the small move the large
text: Every standing body is a balancing act. Your center of gravity sits roughly at hip level, and you stay upright only while it remains over your base of support, the area marked out by your feet. Widen or lower your stance and you are harder to tip; stand tall on narrow feet and a small push can move you. Good posture, with head, spine, and hips in line, lets force pass through your skeleton instead of bending you.

Grappling arts turn these facts into method. Judo teaches kuzushi, breaking the partner's balance, before anything else. A person whose weight has been drawn onto the toes or rocked back onto the heels can no longer push back with full strength, so the throw that follows takes little force. Kano's students learned to add to an opponent's push or pull rather than meet it head-on.

Leverage does the rest. Torque equals force times distance from the pivot, so a grip far from the fulcrum multiplies effort. A joint lock works because it sets your whole body, used as a lever, against one isolated joint. Strength still matters, but structure and timing let it go further.
